en_revised: The country of Īraṇaparvata (伊爛拏鉢伐多國) is over three thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country borders the Gaṅgā River to the north and is over twenty *li* in circuit. The crops are lush and productive, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. There are more than ten monasteries with over four thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are more than twenty deva temples where followers of various heterodox sects live together. Recently, a neighboring king deposed the ruler of this country and bestowed the capital city upon the community of monks. Within this city, two monasteries were built, each housing nearly one thousand monks, both of which study the Hīnayāna Sarvāstivāda school.  Beside the great city, overlooking the Gaṅgā River, is Mount Īraṇa, which exhales mists and clouds that obscure the sun and the moon. From ancient times to the present, immortals and sages have followed one another to dwell there in meditation, and there is now a deva temple that still observes the traditional rites. In the past, the Tathāgata also resided here and preached the profound Dharma extensively for devas and humans. To the south of the great city is a stūpa where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the three past Buddhas. Not far to the west of the walking paths of the three Buddhas is a stūpa; this is the birthplace of the bhikṣu Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (室縷多頻設底拘胝) (in Chinese, "Heard of Two Hundred Koṭis" [聞二百億]; the old translation "Koṭikarṇa" [億耳, "Koṭi-Ear"] is wrong). In the past, there was a wealthy and noble elder in this city who had a child late in life. to the one who then brought him the news he at once gave two hundred koṭis of gold coins, and thus he named his son Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (He who heard of two hundred koṭis). By the time he reached adulthood, he had never once walked upon the ground, and thus the hair on the soles of his feet was over a foot long, lustrous, fine, and soft, with a color like yellow gold. Cherishing this child, his parents provided him with every kind of luxury; from his residence all the way to the Snow Mountains, post-stations were linked together and servants lined the roads, so that whenever a rare medicine was required, the word was passed along and the item delivered in succession, arriving in no time at all—such was the extent of his great wealth. The World-Honored One, knowing that his roots of goodness were about to sprout, commanded Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) to go and convert him. Upon arriving at his gate, he found no way to announce himself. The elder’s family worshipped the Sun Deity, and every morning they would face east to bow. At that time, the Venerable One used his supernatural powers to descend from the solar disc and stand before them. The elder’s son, suspecting he was the Sun Deity, offered him fragrant rice; the Venerable One then returned, and the aroma of the rice filled the entire city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was astonished by the extraordinary fragrance and ordered a messenger to investigate; it was discovered that Maudgalyāyana of the Bamboo Grove Monastery (竹林精舍) had brought the rice from the elder's house, and thus, learning that the elder's son possessed such a wonder, the king summoned him. The elder accepted the command, but pondered how to travel safely. To travel by boat and ply the oars carried the danger of wind and waves; to ride in a carriage or on an elephant brought the fear of stumbling or falling. Thereupon, from his residence to the city of Rājagṛha, he excavated a canal for transport and filled it with mustard seeds, so that the boat could rest securely and be towed along by a long rope. Upon arriving at the city of Rājagṛha, he first paid homage to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said to him, "King Bimbisāra has ordered a messenger to summon you for no other reason than to see the hair on the soles of your feet. If the king wishes to see them, you should sit in the cross-legged position. To extend your feet toward the king is a capital offense according to the laws of the country." The elder's son accepted this instruction and went to the court, where he was led in to have an audience. When the king wished to see the hair, he sat in the cross-legged position; the king praised his courtesy and came to cherish him deeply. Once he was able to return, he went back to the place of the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata (如來) preached the Dharma and offered him instruction; upon hearing it, he was moved to realization and immediately renounced the household life. Thereupon, he practiced with diligent effort, seeking to realize the fruits of enlightenment; he engaged in walking meditation without rest until his feet began to bleed. The World-Honored One said to him, "Good man, when you were at home as a layman, did you know how to play the lute?" He replied, "I did." "If that is so, take this as an analogy. If the strings are too tight, the sound will not be in harmony; if the strings are too loose, the melody will not be refined. Neither too tight nor too loose, the sound is then harmonious. The practitioner of the path is also like this. If one is too urgent, the body becomes exhausted and the mind weary; if one is too lax, the passions expand and the will becomes dissipated." Having received the Buddha's instruction, he followed it faithfully, and before long, he attained the realization of the fruit.

issues: Small Isolated Mountain (小孤山; Skt. asura) → "Skt. asura" invented (previous error recurs); 小孤山 is simply a small isolated hill (Mizutani: 小さな離れ山; Beal: a small isolated mountain); note （即澡瓶也。舊曰軍持，訛略也）: "*junchi*" → give the old transcription as 軍持 (*kundī*), "erroneous and abbreviated"
en_revised: At the western border of the country, south of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River, one reaches the Small Isolated Hill (小孤山). Its layered peaks are lofty and precipitous. In the past, the Buddha spent three months of the rainy season retreat here, subduing the yakṣa Bakula (薄句羅). On a large rock below the southeastern cliff of the mountain, there is a trace of where the Buddha sat, which penetrates the stone by more than an inch; it is five feet two inches long and two feet one inch wide, and a stūpa has been built upon it. Next, to the south on the stone, there is a trace where the Buddha placed his kuṇḍikā (捃稚迦) (that is, a water-jar for washing; formerly called *kundī* [軍持], erroneous and abbreviated), which is more than an inch deep and fashioned with an eight-petaled flower design. Not far to the southeast of the Buddha’s sitting trace is the footprint of the yakṣa Bakula, which is one foot five or six inches long, seven or eight inches wide, and slightly less than two inches deep. Behind the yakṣa’s footprint is a stone seated image of the Buddha, six or seven feet high. Not far to the west is a place where the Buddha walked in meditation. On the summit of the mountain is the former dwelling of the yakṣa. Next, to the north, is a footprint of the Buddha, one foot eight inches long, over six inches wide, and about half an inch deep; there is a stūpa above this trace. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued the yakṣa, causing him to stop killing people and eating meat, and to respectfully receive the Buddha’s precepts, after which he was reborn in the heavens. To the west of this are six or seven hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot. In the great mountain forests at the southern border of the country, there are many wild elephants, which are immense in size.

en_revised: From here, traveling east for more than three hundred li along the southern bank of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, one arrives at the country of Campā (瞻波國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Campā is more than four thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country has the Ganges River to its north and is more than forty li in circuit. The land is low and damp, and the crops are lush and abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest. There are several dozen saṃghārāmas, most of which are dilapidated, with more than two hundred monks who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. There are more than twenty deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. The walls of the capital city are built of brick, several chang high, with lofty and steep foundations and high, precipitous battlements. In the beginning of the kalpa, when human beings first appeared, they lived in the wild and dwelt in caves, not yet knowing of palaces or houses. Later, a celestial maiden descended among humans and, while wandering by the Ganges and bathing in its currents to please herself, she was spiritually moved and became pregnant, eventually giving birth to four sons. They divided Jambudvīpa among themselves, each ruling over a region, building capitals and constructing towns, and marking out boundaries and borders. This city was the capital of one of those sons, and it was the beginning of all the cities in Jambudvīpa.

issues: note （唐言赤泥）: "(Raktamṛttika; Chinese: Red Clay)" → give the transcription 絡多未知 and render the note as "in Chinese, Red Clay" (CBETA reads 絡多未知, 未 for 末; Raktamṛttikā kept); found no errors in the logic or the phrasing → 一聞究覽，辭義無謬: having heard it once he grasped it completely, without error in wording or sense (previous error recurs; Beal: understood it all … without mistake); mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍) → invented gloss, 精舍 = *vihāra* (previous error recurs)
en_revised: Beside the great city is the Raktamṛttikā Monastery (絡多未知僧伽藍) (in Chinese, "Red Clay"). Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and open, and its towers and pavilions are lofty and steep. The highly talented and profoundly learned scholars of the country, as well as those of renowned intelligence, all assemble therein to assist one another through mutual admonition and to cultivate their morality and virtue.  Formerly, before this country believed in the Buddha-dharma, there was a heretic from South India who bound his belly with copper plates, wore a bright torch upon his head, and, leaning on a staff, walked with proud strides into this city, where he struck the drum of debate and sought to engage in discussion. Someone asked him, "Why do you wear a torch on your head and plates on your belly?" He replied, "My learning and skills are so vast that I fear my belly might burst; I pity the ignorance of others, which is why I carry this light."  Ten days passed, and no one came to question him. They inquired among the eminent and wise, but there was no one who could match him. The king said, "Within the borders of this realm, can there be no wise and enlightened men? To leave a guest's challenge unanswered is a deep shame for the country. We should search further and inquire among those living in seclusion."  Someone said, "In the great forest there is an extraordinary man who calls himself a śramaṇa; he is dedicated to arduous study and has lived here in quiet seclusion for a long time. Were he not one who embodies the Dharma and accords with virtue, how could he live like this?"  The king heard this and went in person to invite him. The śramaṇa replied, "I am a man of South India staying here as a traveler; my learning is superficial, and I fear I may fall short of what you have heard. However, I dare to accept your command and will no longer firmly decline. If I am not defeated in the debate, I request that you build a monastery, gather monks together, and glorify and promote the Buddha-dharma." The king said, "I respectfully hear your words and dare not forget your virtue." The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and went to the site of the debate. The non-Buddhist then recited his tenets, totaling more than thirty thousand words. Their meaning was profound and their phrasing concise; they encompassed all names and characteristics, capturing the sight and hearing of the audience. The śramaṇa, having heard them once, comprehended them completely, without error in wording or meaning, and with a few hundred words, he debated and refuted them, then questioned the non-Buddhist on his tenets. The non-Buddhist, his arguments exhausted and his logic defeated, sealed his mouth and could not respond. Having been refuted in his reputation, he retreated in shame. The king deeply respected the śramaṇa’s virtue and built this monastery; from that time thereafter, the Buddha-dharma was widely propagated. Not far from the side of the monastery is a stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王); in the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for seven days to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. Beside it is a *vihāra* (精舍), the place where the past four Buddhas left traces of sitting and walking in meditation. There are several stūpas, all of which are places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, and they were built by King Aśoka.

en_revised: From here, traveling southwest into a vast wilderness with deep forests and giant trees that reached the sky and obscured the sun, one proceeds for one thousand four or five hundred *li* to the country of Kaliṅga (羯𩜁伽國) (Original note: 𩜁 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 力甑) (in the region of South India). The country of Kaliṅga is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty *li* in circuit. Crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant; forests and marshes stretch continuously for hundreds of *li*. It produces dark wild elephants, which are prized by neighboring countries. The climate is hot, and the customs are impetuous and violent; the people are by nature impatient and fierce, yet they value faith and righteousness. Their speech is rapid and light, their tone is simple and direct, and their diction and style are quite different from those of Central India. Few believe in the true Dharma, and most follow non-Buddhist paths. There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than one hundred *deva* temples, and the number of heterodox practitioners is very great, most of whom are followers of the Nirgrantha. In former times, the country of Kaliṅga was prosperous and densely populated, with shoulders rubbing and wheel hubs clashing, and the raising of sleeves would form a curtain. A sage possessing the five supernatural powers was dwelling in the rocks and cultivating purity; because people insulted and provoked him, he lost his supernatural powers and used evil spells to slaughter the people of the country, leaving no one, young or old, and destroying both the wise and the foolish. Human habitation was cut off for many years. Gradually, people have moved back, but it is still not fully populated; therefore, the number of households in this country is currently small. Not far south of the city is a *stūpa* more than one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas.

en_revised: From here, traveling northwest through mountains and forests for over 1,800 li, one reaches the country of Kosala (憍薩羅國) (in the region of Central India). The country of Kosala is over 6,000 li in circumference, with mountain ranges encircling its borders and forests and marshes connected throughout. The capital city of the country is over 40 li in circumference. The soil is rich and fertile, and the land is highly productive. Villages and hamlets look out upon one another, and the households are prosperous and substantial. The people are large in stature and dark in complexion. Their customs are fierce and impetuous, and their nature is brave and violent. They believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings, and they are highly skilled in the arts. The king is a Kṣatriya. He reveres the Buddha-Dharma and is deeply compassionate and far-reaching in his benevolence. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas, and the number of monks is just under ten thousand; all of them study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are over seventy Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, and beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata once manifested great supernatural powers at this place to subdue non-Buddhists. Later, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) resided in this saṃghārāma. At that time, the king of this country was named Sātavāhana (娑多婆訶) (in Chinese, "Leading the Righteous"). He cherished and respected Nāgārjuna, and he guarded the gates of his residence. At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) came from the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) to seek a debate, and he said to the gatekeeper, "I would be grateful if you would announce my visit." The gatekeeper then went to report this. Nāgārjuna, already well aware of his reputation, filled a bowl to the brim with water and instructed his disciple, saying, "Take this water and show it to that Deva." When Deva saw the water, he silently dropped a needle into it. The disciple took the bowl and returned, feeling puzzled. Nāgārjuna asked, "What did he say?" The disciple replied, "He said nothing, but merely dropped a needle into the water." Nāgārjuna said, "How wise he is, this man! To know the subtle is divine; to perceive the minute is to be second only to a sage. With such great virtue, he should be invited in immediately." The disciple asked, "What does this mean? Is this what you call the marvelous eloquence of silence?" Nāgārjuna said, "Water takes the shape of its container, whether square or round; it adapts to the purity or turbidity of its surroundings; it permeates everywhere without gaps, and its clarity is unfathomable. I showed him the bowl filled to the brim to signify that my learning is complete; he dropped a needle into it, thereby exhausting its depths. This is no ordinary person; he should be summoned at once." Nāgārjuna’s demeanor was awe-inspiring and commanded respect; all who spoke with him would bow their heads in submission. Deva had long admired his reputation and had long hoped to request instruction. Just as he was about to become a student, he first wished to display his own keen intellect, yet he was also intimidated by Nāgārjuna’s majesty. He ascended the hall, sat to one side, and they discussed the profound mysteries all day long, their discourse clear and lofty. Nāgārjuna said, "Your scholarship surpasses the world and your brilliant eloquence outshines your predecessors. I am but a feeble old man, and meeting such a talented youth truly allows me to pour the contents of my vessel into another and keep the lamp of transmission burning without end; the propagation of the Dharma depends on such a person. I hope you will move to the front seat so that we may discuss the profound mysteries." Upon hearing this command, Deva, who had been confident in his own mind, prepared to open the storehouse of his arguments and first roam the garden of debate. He raised his points and looked up to challenge the meaning, but suddenly catching sight of Nāgārjuna’s majestic countenance, he forgot his words and fell silent. He moved his seat back, acknowledged his fault, and requested to become his student. Nāgārjuna said, "Sit down again. I shall now bestow upon you the most perfect and wonderful truth, the authentic teaching of the Dharma King." Deva prostrated himself, his five limbs touching the ground, and with a single mind surrendered his life, saying, "From this moment on, I dare to follow your instructions." Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was well-versed in the arts of medicine; by consuming elixirs to nourish his life, he lived for several hundred years, his spirit and appearance showing no signs of decline. The king, Sātavāhana (引正王), having obtained the wonderful medicine, also lived for several hundred years. The king had a young son who said to his mother, "At this rate, when will I ever be able to succeed to the throne?" His mother replied, "Judging by the present situation, there is no prospect. Your father the king has already lived for several hundred years, and many of his descendants have already grown old and died. This is all due to the power of Nāgārjuna’s merit and the efficacy of his medical arts. If the Bodhisattva were to pass away, the king would surely perish. Now, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva possesses vast wisdom and profound compassion; he provides for all living beings and regards his own life as something to be cast aside. You should go to him and try to beg for his head. If you can fulfill this intention, your wish will be granted." The prince respectfully obeyed his mother’s command and came to the monastery; the gatekeepers were awestruck and fearful, so he was able to enter. At that time, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was chanting and walking in meditation. Suddenly seeing the prince, he stopped and asked, "For what reason have you come to the monastery this evening, appearing so anxious and fearful, and rushing here in such haste?" The prince replied, "I have received the words of my compassionate mother, which touched upon those who practice the virtue of giving. I had thought that for all living beings, life is a precious treasure, and that in the words and maxims of the scriptures, there has never been anyone who lightly cast aside their physical body to bestow it upon those who seek it. But my compassionate mother said: 'It is not so. The Sugatas of the ten directions and the Tathāgatas of the three ages, from the time they first resolved their minds until they attained the fruit of enlightenment, diligently sought the Buddha-way and practiced the precepts and forbearance. Some threw their bodies to feed hungry beasts, some cut their flesh to save a dove; King Candraprabha gave his head to a Brahmin, and King Maitrībala gave his blood to satisfy hungry Yakṣas; examples such as these are truly difficult to enumerate fully. In seeking the sages of the past, what age has been without such people?' Now, Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) is firm in his noble ambitions. I have a request for a human head to use, but though I have sought one for many years, no one has yet offered theirs. If I were to commit a violent robbery and murder, the burden of my sins would be all the greater; to cruelly harm the innocent would make my defiled virtue manifest. Only you, Bodhisattva, who practice the holy path and look toward the distant fruit of Buddhahood, whose compassion moistens all sentient beings and whose kindness reaches the boundless, treat life as lightly as a floating bubble and hold your body as cheaply as rotten wood. Do not violate your original vow, but grant what I request!" Nāgārjuna said: "Yes, these words are indeed true! I seek the holy fruit of Buddhahood and I learn from the Buddha the ability to renounce all. This body is like an echo, this body is like a bubble; it circulates through the four types of birth and comes and goes through the six realms. Bound by a long-standing great vow, I will not oppose the desires of living beings. However, Prince, there is one thing that is not possible; what shall be done about it? Once my body is finished, your father will also perish. Considering this, who could save him?" Nāgārjuna paced about and looked around, seeking a way to end his life. He cut his own throat with a blade of dry cogon grass as if with a sharp sword, and his head was severed from his body. Seeing this, the prince was terrified and fled. The gatekeeper went up and reported the matter, detailing the beginning and the end; upon hearing this, the king was overcome with grief and, as a result, he also passed away.
