en_revised: Three hundred or more li southwest of the country, one arrives at the mountain of Bhramaragiri (跋邏末羅耆釐山) (in Chinese, "Black Bee"). It rises abruptly and loftily, with precipitous peaks and cliffs; having neither slopes nor valleys, it appears to be a single solid rock. King Sātavāhana (引正王) excavated this mountain for the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) to establish a monastery (saṃghārāma). Ten or more li from the mountain, a tunnel was excavated; directly beneath the mountain, they carved upward into the rock. Within it are long corridors and eaves, lofty terraces and multi-storied pavilions; the pavilions have five tiers, and each tier has four courtyards, all containing shrines (精舍) where golden images of the Buddha's size have been cast with exquisite craftsmanship, while the remaining decorations consist entirely of gold and jewels. From the high peaks of the mountain, a waterfall pours down, flowing around the multi-storied pavilions and winding through the corridors and verandas. Windows open through to the outside, letting light illuminate the interior. Initially, when King Sātavāhana was building this monastery, the labor force was exhausted and the treasury was empty; with the work not yet half finished, his heart was filled with deep sorrow. Nāgārjuna said to him, "Great King, why are you so burdened with worry?" The king replied, "I have given rise to a great aspiration and ventured to establish a supreme field of merit, hoping it would remain firm forever until the coming of Maitreya (慈氏). With the work not yet finished and the financial resources exhausted, I am constantly filled with this regret, sitting and waiting for the dawn." Nāgārjuna said, "Do not worry. The merit of cultivating such supreme goodness is inexhaustible; if one has raised a vast vow, there is no worry that it will not be fulfilled. Return to the palace today and enjoy yourself to the fullest; tomorrow morning, go out for an excursion, travel through the mountains and fields, and then come here to discuss the construction." The king, having received these instructions, followed them accordingly. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) used a miraculous medicine, dripping it onto large rocks, which all turned into gold. When the king saw the gold during his excursion, he rejoiced in his heart and words; he drove his carriage back to Nāgārjuna’s place and said, "During my outing today, I was deluded by spirits and ghosts, for I repeatedly saw heaps of gold amidst the mountains and forests." Nāgārjuna replied, "It was not a delusion of ghosts. It is the result of your utmost sincerity that this gold has appeared. You should take and use it immediately to complete your noble undertaking." He then proceeded with the construction, and when the work was finished, there was still a surplus. Thereupon, in each of the five tiers, he cast four large golden statues, and the remainder was still abundant, filling the treasuries. He summoned one thousand monks to reside within and perform rites and recitations. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna collected and classified the teachings proclaimed by Śākyamuni Buddha and the treatises composed by various Bodhisattvas, storing them within. Thus, the first tier at the top housed only Buddha images and various scriptures and treatises; the fifth tier at the bottom was for the residence of lay servants (淨人) and the storage of property and miscellaneous goods; and the three middle tiers were the lodgings for the monks. I have heard from the records of former sages that after King Sātavāhana had completed the construction, the cost of salt consumed by the workers was calculated to be nine koṭis (koṭi is, in Chinese, 億, a hundred million) of gold coins. Thereafter, the monks fell into disputes and went to the king to seek arbitration. At that time, the lay servants said to one another, "Since a quarrel has arisen among the monks and their arguments are contradictory, evil men will watch for an opening to destroy the monastery." Consequently, they barred the heavy doors to exclude the monks. From that time on, there has been no monastic community there. Looking at the mountain cliffs from afar, one cannot discern any gate or path. At times, those skilled in medical arts were brought inside to treat illnesses; they were blindfolded upon entering and exiting, and thus did not recognize the route.

issues: From this great forest, traveling south → 從此大林中南行: from here, traveling south through a great forest (earlier error recurs); which was built by the Arhat Ācāra → 並…之所建: both [the monastery and the stūpa] were built by him (並 dropped again, as in the earlier review); note 唐言所行 merged with the Chinese → render as a note after the Chinese name: (阿折羅) (in Chinese, "Conduct"); the earlier slip 所行羅漢伽藍 = 'aforementioned' is fixed
en_revised: From here, traveling south through a great forest for more than nine hundred li, one arrives at the country of Āndhra (案達羅國) (within the borders of South India). The country of Āndhra is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit and is named Vengīpura (瓶耆羅). The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. Their language and tone of speech differ from those of Central India, but as for their written characters, the rules are largely the same. There are more than twenty monasteries and over three thousand monks. There are more than thirty Deva temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous. Not far from the side of Vengīpura city is a large monastery with multi-storied pavilions and layered terraces, the craftsmanship of which exhausts the possibilities of carving; the sacred images of the Buddhas are of exquisite and ingenious design. In front of the monastery is a stone stūpa, several hundred feet high; both were built by the Arhat Ācāra (阿折羅) (in Chinese, "Conduct"). Not far to the southwest of the monastery of the Arhat Ācāra is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; in the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifested great supernatural powers, and delivered immeasurable multitudes.

issues: one reaches the solitary hill (Vyāsa) → 至孤山: a solitary hill; the invented 'Vyāsa' recurs from the earlier review; from the monastery of the Arhat → 所行羅漢伽藍: the monastery of the Arhat Ācāra (name dropped); Dignāga's Chinese name and note: add (陳那) before the note (in Chinese, "Bestowed")
en_revised: Traveling more than twenty *li* southwest from the monastery of the Arhat Ācāra, one reaches a solitary hill. On the mountain ridge is a stone *stūpa* where the Bodhisattva Dignāga (陳那) (in Chinese, "Bestowed") composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic). As for the Bodhisattva Dignāga, after the Buddha had passed away, he followed the tradition and donned the dyed robes. His wisdom and vows were vast and great, and his power of discernment was deep and firm. Pitying the world for having no refuge, he contemplated how to propagate the sacred teachings. Considering that the treatises on logic were profound in language and extensive in reasoning, such that students labored in vain and found it difficult to achieve success, he hid his traces in secluded cliffs and settled his spirit in silent meditation, examining the merits and demerits of past works and scrutinizing the verbosity and conciseness of their meanings. At that time, the cliffs and valleys shook and echoed, the mist and clouds changed color, and a mountain god lifted the Bodhisattva up several hundred feet, proclaiming: "In the past, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, guided sentient beings through skillful means and, with a compassionate heart, preached the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, encompassing wonderful principles and investigating subtle words to their depths. Since the Tathāgata entered extinction, the great meaning has been cut off. Now, the Bodhisattva Dignāga, whose merit and wisdom are vast and far-reaching, and who deeply understands the sacred intent, shall once again propagate the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* on this day." The Bodhisattva then emitted a great light, illuminating the darkness. At that time, the king of this country felt deep respect; seeing this manifestation of light, he suspected the Bodhisattva had entered the *vajra-samādhi* and therefore requested that the Bodhisattva certify the fruit of non-arising. Dignāga said: "I have entered meditation to observe and wish to explain the profound scriptures; my heart is set on perfect enlightenment, not on the fruit of non-arising." The king said: "The fruit of non-arising is something all sages admire; it severs the desires of the three realms and provides mastery of the three types of supernormal knowledge—this is a magnificent achievement, and I hope you will realize it quickly." At that time, Dignāga (陳那) was pleased by the king’s request and was about to realize and accept the holy fruit of the *aśaikṣa* (no-more-learning). At that moment, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (妙吉祥菩薩) knew of this and felt it was a pity; wishing to warn him, he snapped his fingers to awaken him and said: "What a pity! How can you abandon the vast and great mind for a narrow and inferior intention, following a desire for individual salvation while discarding the vow to benefit others? If you wish to perform a virtuous benefit, you should widely propagate the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽師地論) composed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩) to guide and encourage later students; the benefit of this is truly great." The Bodhisattva Dignāga respectfully accepted this instruction and followed it faithfully. Thereupon, he pondered deeply and researched extensively the treatises on *hetuvidyā* (logic). Fearing that students might be intimidated by the subtlety of the text and the conciseness of the language, he extracted the essential meanings and synthesized the profound words to compose the *Nyāyamukha* (因門論) in order to guide those who would come after. From this time forward, he propagated the *Yogācāra* (瑜伽), and his flourishing work and disciples were known throughout the world.

issues: They are situated along rivers → 奠川通徑: they regulated (dammed) the streams and opened paths (Mizutani: 川を奠り, Ming ed. 鑿; Beal's English does not translate this clause); not flagged in the earlier review; notes 唐言東山/西山 given as glosses without the Chinese names: acceptable
en_revised: To the east of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Pūrvaśaila (弗婆勢羅) (in Chinese, "Eastern Mountain") Monastery; to the west of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (阿伐羅勢羅) (in Chinese, "Western Mountain") Monastery. These were built for the Buddha by a former king of this country. The streams were regulated and paths opened, with pavilions perched upon cleared cliffs, and long corridors and covered walkways resting against the rocks and joining the peaks; they are guarded by divine spirits and frequented by sages and saints. Within the millennium following the Buddha’s nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would gather each year to enter the summer retreat; on the day the retreat concluded, they would all attain arhatship and depart by rising into the air through their supernatural powers. After the millennium, ordinary and holy monks lived there together. For over a hundred years, there have been no more monks, and the mountain spirits have changed their forms—sometimes appearing as jackals and wolves, other times as apes and monkeys—to terrify travelers; for this reason, the place is desolate and devoid of any monastic community.

issues: It is situated above a river and connected by paths → 奠川通徑: the stream was regulated (dammed) and paths opened (Mizutani: 川を奠り); ordinary people and sages lived there together → 凡、聖同居: ordinary monks and holy ones (arhats) lived together
en_revised: To the west of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (阿伐羅勢羅) (in Chinese, "West Mountain") Monastery, which a former king of this country built for the Buddha. The stream was regulated and paths opened, with cliffs cleared to support pavilions, long corridors, and covered walkways, all resting against the crags and joining the peaks; divine spirits guard and protect it, and sages and saints have frequented it to rest. Within the millennium following the Buddha’s nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would enter the summer retreat there together each year; on the day the retreat concluded, they would all attain arhatship and depart by rising into the void through their supernatural powers. After that millennium, ordinary monks and holy ones lived there together. For the past hundred years or so, there have been no more monks, and the mountain spirits have changed their forms—sometimes appearing as jackals or wolves, other times as apes or monkeys—to terrify travelers. For this reason, the place has become desolate and is devoid of any monastic community.

issues: when I see it, there must be a realization, and I shall proclaim you the teacher of gods and men → 見當有證，稱天人師: when I see it I shall attain realization and be called Teacher of gods and men, i.e. Bhāviveka himself as Buddha (Mizutani: 見たならば必ず證果を得て天人師となろう); the earlier major error recurs; I am diligent and sincere in my thirst for the sun → 渴日勤誠: all day long I strive earnestly (Mizutani: 日ねもす努力しており; Beal: the whole day I...); Hṛdaya-dhāraṇī (Original note: Suixin tuoluoni) → 《隨心陀羅尼》 has no interlinear note in the text; the 'Original note' is invented; Bodhi Tree (Mahā-bodhi) → gloss not in the text; note 唐言清辯 given without the Chinese name: add (婆毘吠伽)
en_revised: Not far to the south of the city is a great mountain crag, the place where the master of treatises Bhāviveka (婆毘吠伽) (in Chinese, Qingbian, "Clear Discrimination") resided in the palace of the Asuras, awaiting the appearance of Maitreya Bodhisattva to attain Buddhahood. The master of treatises possessed a refined character that was vast and far-reaching, and his supreme virtue was profound and deep; outwardly he displayed the attire of the Sāṃkhya, while inwardly he promoted the teachings of Nāgārjuna. Hearing that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla in the country of Magadha was propagating the teachings of the Dharma and had several thousand students, he felt a desire to engage in discussion, so he took up his staff and set out. Upon arriving at the city of Pāṭaliputra, he learned that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla was at the Bodhi Tree. The master of treatises then instructed his disciple, saying: "Go to the place of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla at the Bodhi Tree and convey my words as follows: 'The Bodhisattva propagates the bequeathed teachings and guides the deluded; I have long looked up to your virtue with a humble mind. However, because my past vows have not yet been fulfilled, I have missed the opportunity to pay my respects. As for the Bodhi Tree, I vow not to see it in vain; when I see it, I shall attain realization and be called the Teacher of gods and men.'" The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla said to his messenger: "The human world is like an illusion, and life is like a floating bubble; all day long I strive earnestly and have no time for discussion." Messengers went back and forth, but they never met. After the master of treatises returned to his native land, he reflected in silence: "If Maitreya does not attain Buddhahood, who can resolve my doubts?" Before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, he recited the *Hṛdaya-dhāraṇī* (隨心陀羅尼), abstaining from grain and drinking only water for a period of three years. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva then manifested a wondrous physical form and said to the master of treatises: "What is your aspiration?" He replied, "I wish to preserve this body to wait until I see Maitreya (慈氏)." Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said, "Human life is precarious and fragile, and the world is a floating illusion; you should cultivate superior and virtuous vows to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天), where you may pay homage and meet him more quickly." The master of treatises said, "My will cannot be swayed, and my heart cannot be divided." The Bodhisattva said, "If that is the case, you should go to the mountain cave south of the city of the country of Dhānyakaṭaka (馱那羯磔迦國) to the abode of the Vajrapāṇi (執金剛) deity; if you recite the *Vajrapāṇi-dhāraṇī* (執金剛陀羅尼) with utmost sincerity, this vow shall be fulfilled." The master of treatises then went there and recited it. After three years, the deity asked him, "What is your wish, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The master of treatises said, "I wish to preserve this body to wait until I see Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva directed me to come and request your aid; is it not in your power to fulfill my vow?" The deity then bestowed a secret method upon him and said, "Inside this rock is the Asura Palace (阿素洛宮); if you perform the ritual according to the Dharma and make your request, the stone wall shall open. Once it opens, you may enter and wait there to see him." The master of treatises said, "If I dwell in seclusion and see nothing, how will I know when the Buddha has arisen?" The Vajrapāṇi deity replied, "When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you." The master of treatises accepted this instruction and practiced the recitation with focused intensity. After another three years had passed, without ever having a different thought, he enchanted mustard seeds and struck the rock with them; the stone wall suddenly split open. At that time, hundreds of thousands of people watched, forgetting to return home. The master of treatises (śāstra-master) stepped across the threshold and announced to the crowd, "I have long prayed, waiting to see Maitreya (慈氏); through the protection of the holy spirits, my great vow is now fulfilled. You should all enter here to witness the arising of the Buddha together." Those who heard this were terrified and none dared to step through the entrance, claiming it was a den of venomous snakes and fearing they would lose their lives. After he exhorted them repeatedly, only six people followed him inside. The master of treatises looked back to bid farewell to the crowd and entered with composure. Once he had entered, the stone wall closed back up. The crowd all lamented and sighed, regretting their previous words.

issues: on the route to the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) → 往南海僧伽羅國路: the Chinese name in the first clause is 僧伽羅國; 執師子 is the interlinear note on the second occurrence (correctly rendered there as a note)
en_revised: To the northeast of this mountain, by the seaside, there is a city which is on the route to the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) in the South Sea. I have heard from the local people that if one enters the sea from here and travels southeast for more than three thousand li, one reaches the country of Siṃhala (in the language of the Tang, this means "Holder of Lions"; it is not within the borders of India).

issues: phonetic note （勒鄧反） after 䮚 dropped → render as note
en_revised: In the southeastern corner of the country is Mount Laṅkā (䮚迦山) (Original note: 䮚 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 勒鄧), with its steep cliffs and deep valleys where spirits and ghosts dwell; it is here that the Tathāgata formerly preached the Laṅkā Sūtra (the old name, Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra [楞伽經], is an error).

issues: *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → gloss invented, 精舍 = vihāra (recurs from previous review) (twice); it is said to have been made by the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi / a stūpa said to contain / It is said that the Arhat → 聞二百億羅漢: 聞 is part of the name (Śroṇa-)Viṃśatikoṭi "Heard-of-twenty-billion", not "it is said" (three times); CBETA reads 荼建那補羅, DM's Konkaṇapura kept
en_revised: From the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國), traveling north into the forests and wilderness, passing isolated cities and small towns where bands of brigands harm travelers, one journeys over two thousand *li* to reach the country of Konkaṇapura (荼建那補羅國) (Original note: in the region of South India). The country of Konkaṇapura is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce. The people are dark-complexioned and their temperaments are wild and violent. They are fond of learning and value virtue and the arts. There are over one hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are several hundred *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Beside the royal palace is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, who are truly men of outstanding talent. In the great *vihāra* (精舍) of this monastery, which is over one hundred feet high, is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成太子). It is slightly less than two feet high, adorned with precious jewels, and kept in a jeweled casket. Whenever a fast day arrives, it is brought out and placed on a high seat to be worshipped with incense and flowers, and at times it emits a brilliant light. Beside the city, in a large monastery, there is a *vihāra* over fifty feet high, containing a sandalwood statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩) over ten feet tall. On fast days, it sometimes shines with a divine light; it was made by the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (聞二百億羅漢). Not far to the north of the city is a forest of *tāla* trees, over thirty *li* in circuit. Its leaves are long and broad, and their color is glossy and smooth; all the various countries use them for writing. In the forest there is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas. Beside it is a stūpa containing the bodily relics of the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi. Not far to the east of the city is a stūpa; its base has already collapsed and sunk, and it remains three *zhang* high. According to ancient records, it contains relics of the Tathāgata, and on fast days it sometimes shines with a divine light. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here and manifested his supernatural powers to save the multitudes of living beings. Not far to the southwest of the city is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is here that the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi manifested great supernatural powers here to transform and save living beings. Beside it is a monastery, of which only the foundations remain, which was built by that Arhat.

issues: great mountain (Pravaragiri) → name not in the text (recurs); vihara (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) → gloss invented, 大精舍 = great vihāra (recurs); 阿折羅（唐言所行） note correctly bracketed
en_revised: On the eastern border of the country is a great mountain with overlapping ridges and connected barriers, and layered peaks with sheer cliffs. There is a monastery situated in a deep valley, with lofty halls and spacious chambers built against the cliffs and peaks; its multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces lean against the rocks and face the gully. It was built by the Arhat Ācāra (which means "the one who acts" in the language of the Tang). The Arhat was a man from West India. After his mother passed away, he observed where she had been reborn and saw that she had taken a woman's body in this country. The Arhat then came to this place, intending to guide and transform her, accepting her according to her capacity. He entered the village to beg for food and arrived at the house where his mother had been reborn. When the girl brought food to offer as alms, her milk began to flow; when her relatives saw this, they considered it an ill omen. The Arhat explained the original karmic causes, and the woman then attained the holy fruit. Feeling gratitude for the grace of his birth and cherishing the karmic conditions that brought it about, the Arhat built this monastery to repay her profound virtue. The great vihāra (精舍) of the monastery is over a hundred feet high, and within it is a stone Buddha statue more than seventy feet tall. Above it are seven stone canopies, suspended in the void without any attachments, with a space of more than three feet between each canopy. I have heard from the records of those before me that this is sustained by the power of the Arhat’s vows; others say it is by the power of supernatural faculties; still others say it is the work of medicinal arts. Upon examining the actual records, the cause remains unclear. The four walls of the vihara are carved with stone reliefs depicting the various causal deeds of the Tathāgata when he was formerly practicing the Bodhisattva path. The auspicious signs of his attainment of the holy fruit and the spiritual responses upon his entry into nirvana are all carved in detail, leaving nothing out. Outside the gate of the monastery, there is a stone elephant at each of the four positions: south, north, left, and right. According to the local people, these elephants occasionally roar loudly, causing the earth to tremble. In the past, the Bodhisattva Dignāga (陳那) frequently resided in this monastery.

issues: phonetic note （昌葉反） after 呫 dropped → render as note
en_revised: From here, traveling west for over a thousand li and crossing the Narmada River (耐秣陀河), one reaches the country of Bharukacchapa (跋祿羯呫婆國) (Original note: 呫 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 昌葉) (in the region of South India). The country of Bharukacchapa is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. The land is saline and barren, with sparse vegetation. The people boil seawater to make salt and rely on the sea for their livelihood. The climate is hot, and swirling winds rise up frequently. The local customs are mean and thin, and the people’s nature is deceitful and cunning. They do not study arts or crafts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten sanghārāmas (伽藍) with over three hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together.

issues: note 即南羅國: "also known as the country of Lāṭa" → "that is, the country of Southern Lā[ṭa] (南羅)"; 南 dropped (Mizutani and Beal read 南羅羅, Southern Lāra; CBETA 南羅); monastery (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) → 精舍 = vihāra, gloss invented (recurs); Great Pañcavārṣika Assembly for 無遮大會 → interpretive, lit. "great unrestricted assembly" (mokṣa-mahāpariṣad) (recurs, previous review kept it with a note; revised here); note 唐言戒日 rendered with Chinese inside, acceptable
en_revised: From here, traveling northwest for more than two thousand li, one reaches the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國) (that is, the country of Southern Lāṭa (南羅); within the borders of South India). The country of Mālava is more than six thousand li in circumference. The capital city is more than thirty li in circumference and is situated to the southeast of the Mahī River. The land is fertile, agriculture is flourishing, the vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are abundant. It is particularly suitable for winter wheat, and the people eat mostly cakes and parched grain. The nature of the people is gentle and compliant; they are generally intelligent, their speech is elegant and clear, and their learning and arts are profound. Within the borders of the Five Indias, two countries place great importance on learning: the country of Mālava in the southwest and the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) in the northeast; they value virtue, honor benevolence, and are brilliant and diligent in their studies. However, in this country, both heterodox and orthodox beliefs are practiced. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas with more than twenty thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sammatiya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are several hundred deva temples, and the number of heterodox practitioners is substantial; most of them are followers who smear themselves with ashes. The local records state: sixty years ago, there was a king named Śīlāditya (in Chinese, "Sun of Virtue" (戒日)). His ingenuity and wisdom were brilliant, his talent and learning were vast and sharp, he cherished and nurtured the four types of living beings, and he revered and honored the Three Jewels. From his birth until his death, his countenance never showed anger, and his hands never harmed a living creature. When his elephants and horses drank water, he would have it filtered first, fearing that he might injure the life-force of the water. His benevolence was such as this. During his reign of more than fifty years, wild beasts became familiar with humans, and the people of the entire country refrained from killing. Beside the palace, he built a *vihāra* (精舍) with the utmost craftsmanship and exquisite adornment, and within it were fashioned images of the seven World-Honored Buddhas. Every year, he regularly held a great unrestricted assembly (無遮大會, *mokṣa-mahāpariṣad*), gathering monks from all directions to provide them with the four monastic requisites, whether in the form of the three robes and religious implements, or various rare treasures of the seven precious gems. This tradition has been passed down through successive generations, and this noble practice has never ceased.

issues: He made a four-legged seat for them → 為座四足: he made the images the four legs of his seat (the point of his arrogance) (Beal: made them the feet of his chair; Mizutani likewise) (recurs from previous review); Upon hearing of this, a bhikṣu went to comfort him → 苾芻聞已: the bhikṣu (Bhadraruci himself) (recurs)
en_revised: More than twenty *li* northwest of the great city, one arrives at the Brahmin village (Brāhmaṇagrāma). Nearby is a deep pit; during the autumn and summer, despite heavy and persistent rains that last for ten days, and although it receives many streams, the water never accumulates. Beside it, a small stūpa has been built. According to ancient records, this is the place where a highly arrogant Brahmin fell into hell while still alive. Formerly, in this village, there was a Brahmin who was naturally wise and widely learned, his scholarship surpassing that of the eminent men of his time. He had thoroughly investigated the profound mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, and the abstruse texts of astronomy and mathematics were as clear to him as if he were looking at the palm of his own hand. His character was noble and refined, and his reputation spread far and wide. The king held him in great esteem and respect, and the people of the country honored him. He had thousands of disciples who admired his way and were drawn to his influence. He would often say, "I have appeared in this world to expound the sacred and guide the ordinary; neither the sages of the past nor the philosophers of the future can compare to me. People are all swept up in following Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha; they propagate their doctrines, paint their images, and vie with one another to offer them worship. Now, since my virtue exceeds theirs and my fame dominates the age, if I do not do something different, how can I manifest my greatness?" He then used red sandalwood to carve images of Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha. He made them the four legs of his seat, and wherever he went, he carried it with him. Such was his arrogance. At that time, in Western India, there was a bhikṣu named Bhadraruci (in Chinese, "Virtuous Love" [賢愛]), who had attained the pinnacle of *hetuvidyā* (logic) and had deeply exhausted the study of heterodox doctrines. His moral conduct was pure and refined, the fragrance of his precepts was intense, and he was possessed of few desires and contentment, seeking nothing from the world. Upon hearing of this, he sighed and said, "Alas! The times are devoid of men, allowing that foolish fellow to dare to practice such wicked deeds." Thereupon, he shouldered his khakkhara (monk's staff) and traveled from afar, arriving in this country, where he fully explained his long-held intention to the king. When the king saw his tattered robes, he did not feel much respect in his heart, yet he esteemed his ambition and reluctantly accorded him the proper courtesies. He then set up a debate seat and informed the Brahmin. The Brahmin heard this and laughed, saying, "Who is that person, that he dares to harbor such an ambition?" He ordered his followers to come to the debate arena, and hundreds of thousands of people gathered before and behind to listen. Bhadraruci wore his tattered, old robes and spread out grass to sit upon. The Brahmin sat perched upon the seat he had brought, denouncing the true Dharma and expounding his heterodox doctrines. The bhikṣu’s clear eloquence flowed like a stream, circling back and forth in argument. After a long time, the Brahmin admitted defeat. The king then said to him, "You have long abused a false reputation, deceiving your superiors and confusing the masses. The ancient codes record that one who loses a debate must be executed." He intended to use a red-hot iron seat to make him sit upon it. The Brahmin, in dire straits, surrendered and begged for his life. Bhadraruci took pity on him and petitioned the king, saying, "Great King, your benevolence and propriety are known far and wide, and your praises fill the roads; you should spread compassionate nurturance rather than practicing cruelty. Forgive his inadequacies and let him go as he pleases." The king ordered him to ride a donkey and announce his defeat throughout the city and its suburbs. The Brahmin, ashamed of this humiliation, became enraged and vomited blood. Upon hearing of this, the bhikṣu went to comfort him, saying, "Your learning encompasses both internal and external doctrines, and your reputation is known far and wide; you should clearly understand the nature of honor and disgrace, and when to advance or retreat. As for fame, what reality does it possess?" The Brahmin, filled with resentment, bitterly reviled the bhikṣu, slandered the Mahāyāna, and spoke with contempt of the ancient sages. Before his words had even died away, the earth split asunder, and he fell alive into the pit; the traces of this event still remain.

issues: note （南印度境） merged into the running text ("which is within the borders of South India") → render as note
en_revised: From here, traveling southwest into a maritime bay and then northwest for two thousand four or five hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Aṭali (阿吒釐國) (within the borders of South India). The country of Aṭali is more than six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and precious treasures are accumulated in abundance. Although agriculture is practiced, the people make their living through trade. The land is sandy and saline, and flowers and fruits are scarce. It produces the black pepper tree, the leaves of which resemble those of the Sichuan pepper. It also produces the frankincense tree, the leaves of which resemble those of the flowering pear. The climate is hot, and there is much wind and dust. The nature of the people is shallow and fickle; they value wealth and despise virtue. Their script, language, customs, and laws are largely the same as those of the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). Most do not believe in merit, and even among those who do, they revere and serve the heavenly deities. There are more than ten temples, where various heterodox sects dwell together.

issues: one hundred *yuta* (hundreds of millions) → 百億 = a hundred koṭis; "yuta" unwarranted (recurs from previous review); note 即比羅羅國: CBETA 比羅羅, DM's "Bīlala" kept (Mizutani emends to 北羅羅 "Northern Lāra"; Beal: Northern Lo-lo)
en_revised: From here, traveling north for more than one thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國) (also called the country of Bīlala; it is within the borders of Southern India). The country of Valabhī is more than six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than thirty *li* in circuit. The produce of the land, the suitability of the climate, and the customs and human nature of the people are the same as in the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). The inhabitants are prosperous, and the households are wealthy; there are more than one hundred families who have accumulated wealth of a hundred *koṭi*s. Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered in this country. There are more than one hundred *saṃghārāma*s, with more than six thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the heterodox sects are very numerous. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country; therefore, King Aśoka erected markers and built *stūpa*s at all the places where the Buddha stopped. The sites where the three past Buddhas sat, walked, and preached the Dharma are interspersed among them. The current king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is the nephew of the former King Śīlāditya of the country of Mālava and the son-in-law of the current King Śīlāditya of the country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國). His name is Dhruvabhaṭa (杜魯婆跋吒) (in the language of Tang, this means "Permanently Intelligent"). His temperament is impetuous, and his wisdom and strategy are shallow. However, he has pure faith in the Three Jewels. Every year, he holds a great assembly for seven days, offering rare treasures and superior delicacies to the community of monks. He gives away the value of the three robes and medicines, as well as rare and precious treasures of the seven kinds, and then redeems them at double their price. He values virtue and honors the worthy; he follows the Way and respects learning. He shows special reverence and respect to high-ranking monks from distant regions. Not far from the city is a great monastery (saṃghārāma) established by the Arhat Ācāra, where the Bodhisattvas Guṇamati and Sthiramati resided and composed treatises that are widely circulated.

issues: most of the inhabitants are followers who smear themselves with ash → 天祠數十，多是塗灰之侶: [the deva-temple people] are mostly ash-smearers; "inhabitants" is DM's addition (recurs from previous review)
en_revised: From here, traveling northward for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Maheśvarapura (in the region of Central India). The country of Maheśvarapura is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Ujjayanī (鄔闍衍那國). They revere and honor non-Buddhist paths and do not believe in the Buddha-Dharma. There are several dozen Deva temples, most of them belonging to followers who smear themselves with ash. The king is of the Brahmin caste and does not have much faith or respect for the Buddha-Dharma.

issues: keeping their traces far from the mountain forests → 遠迹山林: withdraw far into the mountains and forests (sense reversed; recurs from previous review); stubbornly hold to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) views → 專執小見: narrow views, not a term for Hīnayāna (recurs); Upagupta (優波毱多) → the text writes 烏波毱多
en_revised: From here I returned to the country of Gurjara (瞿折羅國), then traveled north through wild wastes and dangerous deserts for over one thousand nine hundred li, crossed the great Sindhu (信度) River, and arrived at the country of Sindhu (in the territory of Western India). The country of Sindhu is over seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city is named Viṣambhapura (毘苫婆補羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain crops and is abundant in winter wheat; it produces gold, silver, and brass, and is suitable for raising cattle, sheep, camels, and mules. The camels are small and have only one hump. It produces much red salt, the color of which is like red stone, as well as white salt, black salt, and white rock salt; people in distant foreign lands use these as medicine. The people are fierce and straightforward by nature, frequently quarrel, and are prone to slander. They are not widely learned, but they deeply believe in the Buddhadharma. There are several hundred monasteries with over ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sammitīya school of the Hīnayāna; for the most part, they are indolent, and their character and conduct are corrupt. However, those who are diligent, virtuous, and good dwell alone in quiet seclusion, withdrawing far into the mountains and forests, and, working day and night without slackening, many attain the holy fruits. There are over thirty Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he is pure and simple by nature and respects the Buddhadharma. In the past, the Tathāgata traveled extensively in this country, and therefore King Aśoka built several dozen stūpas at the sites of the holy traces. The great arhat Upagupta (烏波毱多) frequently traveled to this country to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. At every place he stayed, he marked the sacred traces, either by building a monastery (saṃghārāma) or erecting a stūpa; these rise up here and there, and can be briefly described. Along the side of the Sindhu River (信度河), in the midst of marshes extending over a thousand li, there are several hundred thousand households residing there. Their nature is fierce and violent, and they are devoted solely to killing. They herd cattle to sustain their lives and have no other means of livelihood. Whether male or female, noble or base, they shave their hair and beards and wear the kaṣāya (monastic robes), appearing like bhikṣus while engaging in secular affairs; they stubbornly hold to narrow views and reject the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). I have heard from the records of the ancients: "In the past, the common people of this land were hardened and cruel, devoted only to violence." At that time, an arhat took pity on their fallen state and, in order to transform them, came through the void, manifesting great supernatural powers and displaying rare wonders, causing the multitude to believe and accept his teachings, which he introduced gradually. The people were respectful and pleased, and wished to follow his instructions. The arhat, knowing that the hearts of the multitude were compliant, administered the three refuges to them, calmed their ferocity, caused them to completely cease killing, and had them shave their hair, dye their garments, and respectfully practice the teachings of the Dharma. As the ages grew distant and the world changed with the passage of time, their adherence to goodness faltered, yet the remnants of their old customs were not extinguished; although they wear the robes of the Dharma, they have never possessed the precepts or virtue. Their descendants, generation after generation, have made this their custom.

issues: suitable for growing wheat and barley → 宜宿、麥 (CBETA punctuation): suitable for winter wheat (宿麥); previous error (宿 = śāli) replaced by another wrong reading; note 唐言最勝子: "Most Victorious One" → "Most Victorious Son", and Chinese left inside the note
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for more than seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Parvata (鉢伐多國) (within the borders of Northern India). The country of Parvata is more than five thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous and numerous. It is subject to the country of Takka (磔迦國). There is much early-ripening rice, and it is suitable for winter wheat. The climate is temperate, the customs are simple and honest, the people’s temperament is impetuous and hasty, and their speech contains vulgar expressions. They are deeply learned in the arts and sciences, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks, who study both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings. There are four stūpas, which were built by King Aśoka. There are twenty Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Beside the city is a large monastery with over a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings; this is where the former śāstra master Jinaputra (in Chinese, "Most Victorious Son" (最勝子)) composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*, and it is also the place where the śāstra masters Bhadraruci and Guṇaprabha originally entered the monastic order. This large monastery was burned by celestial fire and is now ruined and desolate.

issues: the *śāli* rice and wheat → 宿、麥 = winter wheat (宿麥) (recurs from previous review); Sthavira-Saṃmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle → 小乘正量部: Sāṃmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle; "Sthavira" not in the text (recurs)
en_revised: Traveling southwest from the country of Sindhu (信度國) for fifteen or sixteen hundred li, one reaches the country of Audumbatira (阿點婆翅羅國) (within the borders of West India). The country of Audumbatira is over five thousand li in circuit. The great capital city is named Khasvara (朅䶩濕伐羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. It is situated in a remote western region, bordering the Sindhu River and adjacent to the shore of the great sea. The buildings are magnificent and contain many precious treasures. Recently, it has had no sovereign and is under the jurisdiction of the country of Sindhu. The ground is low and damp, the soil is saline, and foul weeds grow in abundance. The fields are little cultivated; although all types of grain are present, winter wheat is particularly abundant. The climate is slightly cold, and the winds are fierce and strong. It is suitable for cattle, sheep, camels, mules, and similar livestock. The people are impetuous and do not like to study. Their language differs slightly from that of Mid-India. Their customs are simple and honest, and they revere the Three Jewels. There are more than eighty saṃghārāmas and over five thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Sāṃmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are ten deva temples, mostly inhabited by ash-smearing heterodox ascetics. In the city, there is a temple to Maheśvara (大自在天). The temple is carved and adorned, and the image of the deity is spiritually responsive; ash-smearing heterodox ascetics reside within it. In the past, the Tathāgata traveled extensively in this country, preaching the Dharma to save people and guiding the commoners to benefit the populace; therefore, King Aśoka (無憂王) built six stūpas at the sites of these sacred traces.

issues: Adhyavakila (阿點婆翅羅國) → same country rendered Audumbatira in 11.18; harmonized (both are modern reconstructions of 阿點婆翅羅)
en_revised: Traveling west from here for less than two thousand li, one reaches the country of Laṅgala (狼揭羅國) (within the borders of Western India). The country of Laṅgala measures several thousand li in each of the four directions. The capital city is over thirty li in circumference and is named Sthūlīśvara (窣菟黎濕伐羅). The land is fertile and moist, and crops are abundant. The climate and customs are the same as those of the country of Audumbatira (阿點婆翅羅國). The inhabitants are prosperous and possess many precious treasures. It borders the great ocean and is the route to the country of the Western Women (西女國). There is no great monarch; the people occupy the river valleys and establish themselves independently, not acknowledging the authority of one another, and are subject to the country of Pārsi (波剌斯國). Their writing is largely the same as that of India, though their spoken language differs slightly. They believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred monasteries with more than six thousand monks, who study and practice the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. There are several hundred Deva temples, and the ash-smearing heretics are extremely numerous. Inside the city is a temple of Maheśvara (大自在天), magnificent and grand, which is the place of worship for the ash-smearing heretics.

issues: much wheat and barley → 多宿、麥: much winter wheat (宿麥) (recurs from previous review); Adembasila (*Aṭembasila*) → 阿點婆翅羅, harmonized with 11.18 (Audumbatira); CBETA reads 臂多縶羅 (縶 for 勢), DM's transcription kept
en_revised: Traveling north from the country of Audumbatira (阿點婆翅羅國) for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Pi-to-zhi-luo (臂多縶羅國) (within the borders of Western India). The country of Pi-to-zhi-luo is more than three thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous; they have no great sovereign but are subject to the country of Sindhu (信度國). The land is sandy and saline, and the cold winds are biting. There is much winter wheat, but few flowers or fruits. The customs of the people are fierce and violent. Their language differs from that of Central India. They do not care for the arts or learning, yet they are sincere in their faith. There are more than fifty monasteries with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than twenty *deva* temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing non-Buddhists. In a large forest fifteen or sixteen *li* north of the city, there is a *stūpa* several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Inside it are relics that occasionally emit light. This is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life as a *ṛṣi*, was harmed by a king. Not far to the east of this is an old monastery, which was established by the great arhat Mahākātyāyana. Beside it are the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas, where *stūpas* have been built to mark the sites.

issues: three hundred li → 三百餘里: more than three hundred li; millet and wheat → 宿、麥 = winter wheat (recurs from previous review); *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) → gloss invented, 精舍 = vihāra (recurs); previous major (聽 "listened") now corrected to "permitted"; note 唐言靴 correctly bracketed
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Avaṇḍa (阿軬荼國) (in the region of West India). The country of Avaṇḍa is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. There is no great monarch; it is subject to the country of Sindhu (信度國). The land is suitable for agriculture; winter wheat is especially abundant, while flowers and fruits are scarce, and trees and vegetation are sparse. The climate is windy and cold, and the nature of the people is fierce and impetuous. Their speech is simple and plain, and they do not value academic pursuits, yet they are pure and faithful in their devotion to the Three Jewels. There are over twenty saṃghārāmas with more than two thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are five Deva temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing heretics. Not far to the northeast of the city, in a large bamboo grove, are the remaining foundations of a saṃghārāma; this is where the Tathāgata once permitted the bhikṣus to wear *jīvashī* (亟縛屣) (in Tang language: boots). Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; although the base has collapsed, it is still over one hundred feet high. In the *vihāra* (精舍) beside it, there is a standing Buddha image made of blue stone, which sometimes emits divine light on fast days. Eight hundred paces further south, in the forest, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. The Tathāgata once stayed here; because the night was cold, he covered himself with his three robes, and the next morning, he permitted the bhikṣus to wear quilted robes. In this forest, there is a place where the Buddha walked in meditation. There are also several stūpas, arranged like fish scales facing one another, which are the places where the four past Buddhas sat. Inside that stūpa are the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata, which often emit divine light on fast days.

issues: note （錫苟反，下同） 'pronounced like si and gou, and so on below' → a fanqie: 䅳 is read with the initial of 錫 and the final of 苟; 'likewise below' (Beal: no note); Mount Aruṇa lacks its Chinese 阿路猱山
en_revised: The country of Jaguḍa (漕矩吒國) is over seven thousand li in circuit. The great capital city of the country is called Ghasna (鶴悉那), which is over thirty li in circuit; sometimes the capital is at the city of Ghasala (鶴薩羅城), which is also over thirty li in circuit, and both are steep, rugged, and well-fortified. The mountains and rivers are undulating, and the fields and ridges are high and dry. Crops are sown in their proper seasons, winter wheat grows in abundance, vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are flourishing. The land is suitable for saffron (欝金香), and it produces the hingu herb (興瞿草), which grows in the Rāmēndu (羅摩印度) valley. In the city of Ghasala, there are gushing springs that flow in various directions, which the people of the country utilize to irrigate their fields. The climate is cold and harsh, with frequent frost and snow. The people are impulsive by nature and their dispositions are often deceitful. They are fond of learning arts and possess many technical skills; they listen but do not understand, yet they can recite tens of thousands of words a day. Their script and language differ from those of other countries. They often embellish empty talk and accomplish few practical results. Although they worship the hundred gods, they revere and honor the Three Jewels. There are several hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The present king is sincere in his faith, having inherited the throne through successive generations; he is devoted to performing meritorious deeds, and is intelligent and fond of learning. There are more than ten stūpas built by King Aśoka (無憂王). There are several dozen deva temples, where followers of different sects live together. Most of the people are non-Buddhists, and their disciples are extremely numerous; they worship the deity Śuna (䅳那) (Original note: 䅳 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 錫苟, i.e. the initial of 錫 with the final of 苟; likewise below). This deity formerly moved from Mount Aruṇa (阿路猱山) in the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國) to reside in Mount Śunāśīra (䅳那呬羅山) on the southern border of this country, where he displays his power, bestows blessings, and commits acts of violence and evil; those who believe and pray to him have their wishes fulfilled, while those who despise him incur calamity. Thus, those far and near revere him, and those high and low stand in awe of him. The rulers, ministers, officials, and commoners of neighboring countries with different customs gather without appointment on auspicious days each year; they bring gold, silver, and rare treasures, or offer cattle, horses, and domestic animals, competing to present offerings to express their sincerity. Consequently, gold and silver are spread upon the ground and sheep and horses fill the valleys, yet no one dares to covet them, as all are intent only on making offerings. Those who follow non-Buddhist paths and practice asceticism with a disciplined heart are granted incantations by the celestial deity; the non-Buddhists who practice them find them highly effective, and those treated for illnesses are often healed.

issues: note （居勿反） after 屈 dropped → fanqie: 屈 is read with the initial of 居 and the final of 勿
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast, crossing ridges and traversing valleys along dangerous canyon paths for more than three hundred li, one reaches the country of Kuraṇa (屈浪拏國) (Original note: 屈 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 居勿). The country of Kuraṇa is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than two thousand li in circumference. The land, topography, and climate are the same as those of the country of Yambagan (淫薄健國). The customs lack laws and regulations, and the people’s nature is base and violent. Most do not cultivate merit, and few believe in the Buddha-Dharma. Their appearance is ugly and wretched, and they mostly wear felt and coarse wool. There are rocky mountains that produce much gold essence; one must chisel and break the stones to obtain it. The monasteries are few, and the monks are also scarce. Their king is simple and sincere, and he reveres and honors the Three Jewels.

issues: note 'Zhenkan [鑊侃]' → the text has 鎮偘 (DM miswrote the characters); 'saṃghārāmas' fine
en_revised: From here, traveling northeast, climbing mountains and entering valleys along a difficult and dangerous path for over five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國) (Original note: also called Zhenkan [鎮偘], and also called Humi [護蜜]). The country of Dharmasthiti lies between two mountains and is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over one thousand five or six hundred li from east to west, and four to five li wide from north to south, while at its narrowest it does not exceed one li. It borders the Vakṣu River (縛芻河), winding and twisting with uneven mounds and hillocks; sand and stones drift and spread, and the cold winds are harsh and piercing. They only plant wheat and beans; there are few forests and a lack of flowers and fruits. They produce many good horses; although the horses are small in stature, they are enduring in running and traveling. The customs lack propriety and righteousness, and the people’s nature is fierce and violent. Their appearance is base and ugly, and they wear felt and coarse wool garments. Their eyes are mostly emerald green, which is different from other countries. There are more than ten saṃghārāmas, but the number of monks is small.

Pravaragiri) → not in the text (recurs from previous review); note 唐言漢日天種 'the celestial race of the Han' → 'the race of the Han and the Sun-deva' (日天 = sun god; DM itself later has 'Han-Sun-God Clan') (Beal: 'descendants of the Han and Sun-god'); 宜推首惡，或以後誅 'we should identify the ringleader, or perhaps we will be executed later' → we should seek out the culprit, so that he may be executed afterwards (Beal: 'with a view to punish him hereafter'); 不知死地 'not knowing how to face death' → I know not where I shall die
en_revised: From this valley, traveling southeast, one climbs mountains and traverses dangerous paths where there are no human habitations, only much ice and snow. After traveling more than five hundred li, one reaches the country of Kharbanda (朅盤陀國). The country of Kharbanda is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is built upon a large rocky ridge, with the Sītā River (徙多河) at its back, and it is over twenty li in circuit. The mountain ranges are connected, and the valleys and plains are narrow. Grain crops are scarce, but beans and wheat are abundant; trees are sparse, and there is little fruit or flowers. The plains and marshes are desolate, and the cities and towns are empty. The customs lack propriety and righteousness, and the people have little learning or skill. Their nature is fierce and violent, yet they are also brave and valiant. Their appearance is ugly and wretched, and they wear garments of felt and coarse wool. Their script and language are largely the same as those of the country of Khāsa (佉沙國). However, they are sincere in their faith and deeply revere the Buddhadharma. There are more than ten monasteries and over five hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) according to the Sarvāstivāda school. The current king is simple and honest, respects the Three Jewels, is refined and elegant in his demeanor, and is devoted to learning. Since the founding of the kingdom, many years have passed. The people claim to be the descendants of the *Cīna-deva-gotra* (至那提婆瞿呾羅) (Original note: in the language of the Tang, "the race of the Han and the Sun-deva"). The origin of this country was a desolate valley in the Onion Range (Pamirs). Long ago, a king of Persia (波利剌斯) married a princess from the land of Han and was escorting her back when they reached this place. At that time, there was a military rebellion, and the roads to the east and west were blocked. He therefore placed the princess upon an isolated peak, which was extremely steep and dangerous, accessible only by ladders to ascend or descend, and he stationed guards all around to keep watch day and night. Three months passed, and the bandits were finally pacified. When he intended to continue on the road home, the princess was already pregnant. The envoy was terrified and said to his retinue, "The King ordered us to welcome his bride, but we encountered this rebellion; camping in the wild barrens, we cannot even plan for the next morning. Through the virtue of our King, the baleful atmosphere has been cleared, and now we are to return to the kingdom, yet the King’s bride is pregnant. Considering this, we are in distress, not knowing where I shall die; we should seek out the chief culprit, so that he may be executed afterwards." There was a clamor of questioning, but no one could determine the truth. At that time, a maidservant said to the envoy, "Do not blame one another; it was a divine encounter. Every day at high noon, a man would arrive here on horseback, descending from the solar disc." The envoy said, "If that is the case, how can we clear ourselves of this guilt? If we return, we will surely be executed; if we stay, we will also be punished. With advancement or retreat being thus, what is the proper course of action?" They all agreed, "This matter is not trivial; who would willingly face such severe punishment? Let us await our fate outside the borders and delay for a while."  Thereupon, they built a palace and quarters on the stone peak, with a circumference of more than three hundred paces. They built a city wall around the palace, established the woman as sovereign, and instituted officials and laws. When the time came, she gave birth to a son, whose appearance was beautiful and refined. The mother managed the affairs of state, and the son assumed the royal title. He could fly through the void and control the wind and clouds; his majesty and virtue reached far and wide, and his reputation and teachings spread to distant lands. Neighboring regions and foreign countries all paid him homage. When the king died at a ripe old age, he was buried in a stone chamber within a large mountain over a hundred *li* southeast of this city. His corpse was preserved like a mummy and remains intact to this day; resembling an emaciated person, he looks as if he were fast asleep, and his clothes are changed periodically while incense and flowers are constantly placed before him. His descendants have continued through the generations down to the present day. Because in the time of their ancestor, the mother was a person from the land of Han (China) and the father was of the seed of the Sun God, they call themselves the "Han-Sun-God Clan." However, their royal family resembles the people of the Middle Kingdom (China) in appearance; they wear square crowns as head ornaments and dress in foreign clothing. Later, their descendants declined and were pressured by powerful states. King Aśoka (無憂王) appeared in the world and built a stupa within their palace. The king later moved his residence to the northeast corner of the palace and converted his former palace into a monastery for the venerable Shastra Master Kumāralāta (童受論師), with lofty, spacious terraces and pavilions and solemn, majestic Buddha statues. The venerable master was a native of the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國); he was brilliant from childhood, renounced the secular world early, devoted his mind to the scriptures, and focused his spirit on the profound mysteries, daily reciting thirty-two thousand words and writing another thirty-two thousand. Thus, his learning surpassed the scholars of his time, and his fame was high in the world; he established the True Dharma, refuted heterodox views, and his lofty discourses were clear and elevated, leaving no difficulty unaddressed, so that he was universally esteemed throughout the five Indias. The treatises he authored number several dozen; they are all widely circulated and studied, for he is the founding master of the Sautrāntika school. At that time, there was Aśvaghoṣa in the east, Deva in the south, Nāgārjuna in the west, and Kumāralāta in the north; they were known as the "four suns that illuminate the world." Therefore, the king of this country, having heard of the venerable master's great virtue, mobilized his troops to attack the country of Takṣaśilā and obtained him by coercion; he then built this monastery to manifest his reverence.

issues: note （通論反） after 奔 dropped → fanqie: 奔 read with the initial of 通 and the final of 論; name lacks its Chinese 奔穰舍羅
en_revised: To the northeast of the great cliff, crossing ridges and traversing dangerous paths for over two hundred *li*, one arrives at Puṇyaśālā (奔穰舍羅) (Original note: 奔 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 通論; in the Tang language, "House of Merit"). It is situated on the eastern ridge of the Onion Range (葱嶺), amidst four mountains, in a basin over one hundred *qing* in area, sunken in the center. Snow accumulates there throughout winter and summer, and the wind is cold and fierce. The fields and ridges are saline and barren, so crops do not grow; there are no trees, only fine grass. Even during the heat of summer, there is much wind and snow; as soon as travelers enter, clouds and mist arise, and merchant caravans suffer greatly from these hardships and dangers.  I have heard from the elders: once there were merchants with a following of over ten thousand and several thousand camels, carrying goods in pursuit of profit, who encountered wind and snow, and both people and animals perished. At that time, there was a great Arhat in the kingdom of *Kharbanda* (朅盤陀國) who saw them from afar; pitying their peril, he desired to exercise his supernatural powers to rescue them from their plight, but by the time he arrived, the merchants had already perished. He then collected their various treasures, gathered all that remained, constructed a building, stored up provisions, purchased land in neighboring countries, and bought households in border cities to provide relief for those traveling to and fro. Therefore, travelers and merchant caravans today all receive support from this.

issues: 'skilled at weaving fine rugs and carpets' → 工織細㲲氍毺: skilled at weaving fine cotton cloth (㲲) and woollen rugs; note correct (Shule lacks Chinese 疏勒)
en_revised: Traveling north from here for over five hundred li across mountains, gravelly plains, and wilderness, one arrives at the country of Khāsa (佉沙國) (Original note: What was formerly called Shule (疏勒) is actually the name of its capital city. The correct pronunciation should be Śrī-kṛtati; the term Shule is a corruption). The country of Khāsa is over five thousand li in circumference. There is much gravel and sand, and little fertile soil. Agriculture is flourishing, and flowers and fruits are abundant. It produces fine felt and coarse wool, and they are skilled at weaving fine cotton cloth and woollen rugs. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the winds and rains follow their proper seasons. The people are fierce and violent by nature, and their customs are full of deceit; they treat ritual and righteousness lightly, and their learning and arts are superficial. It is their custom to compress the heads of newborn children to make them flat; their appearance is coarse and vulgar, and they have tattooed bodies and green eyes. Their writing system is modeled after that of India; although there have been deletions and corruptions, it still retains the original structure. Their language and tone of speech differ from those of other countries. They are sincerely devoted to the Buddha-dharma and diligently engage in meritorious works. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas with over ten thousand monks, who study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. They do not delve deeply into the principles but mostly recite the texts; therefore, many have mastered the recitation of the Tripiṭaka and the Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra.

issues: 群下勸進 'his subordinates urged him to advance' → urged him to take the throne (勸進 = urge accession); note correct (variant names lack Chinese: 渙那, 于遁, 谿旦, 屈丹, 于闐)
en_revised: Going eastward from here, crossing mountains and valleys for more than eight hundred li, one reaches the country of Gostana (瞿薩旦那國) (in the language of Tang, this means "Earth-Nipple," which is the elegant form of the local name. In the vulgar tongue it is called the country of Huanna; the Xiongnu call it Yudun; the various Hu peoples call it Qidan; and in India it is called Qudan. The old name, Yutian (于闐), is erroneous). The country of Gostana is more than four thousand li in circumference. More than half of it is sand and gravel, and the arable land is narrow and restricted. It is suitable for grain crops and produces many kinds of fruit. It produces rugs and fine felt, and the people are skilled at spinning and weaving silk and pongee. It also produces white jade and black jade. The climate is mild and pleasant, though there are drifting winds and flying dust. The customs value propriety and righteousness, and the people are gentle and respectful by nature. They are fond of learning the arts and are broadly proficient in various skills. The populace is wealthy and happy, and the households are settled in their occupations. The country prizes musical sounds, and the people are fond of singing and dancing. Few wear coarse wool, felt, or furs; most clothe themselves in silk, pongee, and white cotton. Their deportment is refined, and their customs are well-ordered. Their writing and laws are modeled after those of India, though they have slightly altered the style and form, having undergone some evolution. Their language differs from that of other countries. They revere and uphold the Buddha-dharma. There are more than one hundred sanghārāmas (伽藍) and over five thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The king is very brave and martial, respects the Buddha-dharma, and claims to be a descendant of the deity Vaiśravaṇa (毘沙門天). In ancient times, this country was empty and uninhabited, and the deity Vaiśravaṇa resided here. After the crown prince of King Aśoka (無憂王) had his eyes gouged out in the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國), the king angrily rebuked his ministers and exiled the powerful families to the north of the Snow Mountains to dwell among the desolate valleys. These exiles followed their herds and reached the western border of this land, where they elected their leader and established him as king. At that time, a prince from the eastern lands had been banished and had migrated to dwell on the eastern border of this region; his subordinates urged him to assume the throne, and he too proclaimed himself king. As years and months accumulated, their customs and teachings remained disconnected. Each group, while out hunting, encountered the other in the desolate marshes; they inquired about each other’s lineage and consequently disputed who was superior. Anger manifested in their words, and they were about to engage in battle. Someone advised them, saying, "Why be so hasty now? To decide the battle while hunting does not fully display the sharpness of our weapons. It is better to return and prepare our troops, and gather at an appointed time." Thereupon, they turned their carriages and returned, each going back to his own country to drill their horses and soldiers and encourage their troops. When the appointed time arrived, the armies met, and their banners and drums faced one another. The next day they joined battle, and the Western Lord was disadvantaged; consequently, he was pursued in his retreat and his head was cut off. The Eastern Lord, riding the momentum of his victory, pacified and gathered the people of the defeated country, moved his capital to the central region, and began to build city walls. Worried that he lacked land and fearing that he might not succeed, he made a proclamation far and near, asking who knew the geography. At that time, there was an ash-smeared outsider (tīrthika) who carried a large gourd filled with water and stepped forward, saying, "I know the geography." He then let the water flow out in winding curves, returning to where it started, and then he hurried away and suddenly vanished. Following those water marks, the foundations were raised and the construction was successfully completed; this became the seat of government, and it is in this city that the current king has established his capital. The city is not high or steep, yet it is difficult to overcome by attack, and from ancient times until now, no one has been able to conquer it. By the time the king had moved the capital to build this city, established the state, and settled the people, his achievements were complete and he was in the twilight of his old age; yet he had no heir and feared the end of his ancestral line. He then went to the place of the god Vaiśravaṇa (毘沙門天神) to pray for an heir. From the forehead of the god’s statue, an infant was produced; the king took him in his arms and returned to his palace, and the people of the country celebrated. Since the baby would not drink milk, the king feared he would not live long, so he soon returned to the divine shrine to pray again for a way to nourish him. The ground in front of the deity suddenly rose up in the shape of a breast, and the divine child suckled from it until he grew to adulthood. His wisdom and courage surpassed his predecessors, and his moral influence spread far and wide; he then built a divine shrine to honor his ancestor. From that time on, the throne has been passed down through generations, and the kings have ruled the country without the line being broken. Therefore, the divine temple today contains many precious treasures, and offerings and sacrifices are made there without fail. Because he was nourished by the earth-breast, this became the name of the country.
